tagline: A winding prairie road through the country of a managed bison herd
intro: Wildlife Loop Road twists through prairie and ponderosa pine hills in Custer State Park. Travel South Dakota presents this 18-mile State Scenic Byway as a drive through pine-covered hills, rolling prairies and red-walled canyons, with bison and other wildlife along the way. The state park agency allows an hour and a half, with travel time dependent on wildlife jams. The 18 miles form a U rather than a complete loop; returning along the full loop brings the distance to 30 miles.

The herd began with 36 bison bought in 1914. As the population grew, the park developed a management system to protect both the animals and their grazing ground. The official roundup began in 1965; each fall, riders gather the animals for health checks and selection of animals for removal. In December 2017, the Legion Lake Fire crossed Wildlife Loop Road and burned much of the herd’s grazing ground. Afterward, park officials increased their annual debris-clearing area.

Drive from Blue Bell on the western side toward the east entrance along the U-shaped route. Near the southeastern tip, burros are often found beside the road. At the visitor center by the east entrance, a map shows the buffalo’s whereabouts that day.

moments.title: Blue Bell
moments.text: Blue Bell takes its name from the bluebell flowers native to the area. A public recreational lodge was established here in 1925, before the community’s post office opened in 1932. The post office lasted until 1941. The Blue Bell entrance marks the western end of the byway’s 18-mile U.

moments.title: Legion Lake Fire
moments.text: In December 2017, the Legion Lake Fire jumped Wildlife Loop Road. It burned most of the land surrounding the route, including much of the bison herds’ grazing area and its fenced perimeter. Bison and burros were moved into corrals for protection, but injured animals in both herds were later euthanized. Afterward, park officials increased the area cleared of debris each year from 1,000 to 3,000 acres. The fire began when wind brought down a tree onto an active power line. A 2018 grant helped fund reseeding and weeding of the burned ground.

moments.title: The burros
moments.text: The burros often found near the southeastern tip of the loop descend from pack animals used by miners and others in the Black Hills. They beg for snacks from passing vehicles, but park rules prohibit feeding any wildlife.

practical: Blue Bell: The road is open year-round; a South Dakota State Park Entrance License or Temporary Custer State Park pass is required. Winter conditions require careful driving. (checked 2026-10-11)
